g.text: The pub/sub routing table IS the fan-out - so nothing on the hot path knows who is listening
And the service boundaries follow a genuine difference in STATE MODEL, which is the most defensible kind of split.
The location-update path, 333,000 times a second
mobile
client
10M concurrent,
WebSocket, not
HTTP polling
L4 load
balancer
L4 because these are
long-lived TCP; L7
buys nothing and adds
a hop. Sticky, so a
reconnect reuses warm
subscriptions.
WS server A
holds this connection
STATEFUL
1 SET loc:{uid} = (lat,lng,ts)
EX 600
2 append to the history stream
async, fire-and-forget
3 PUBLISH channel:{uid}
ONE publish, any friend count
4 keep an in-memory copy for this user's
own distance calculations
Step 3 is the pivot: ONE publish per
update, not 40 sends. The publisher does
not know or care who is listening - no
friend-list lookup, no connection
registry, no fan-out loop on the sender.
The pub/sub layer's ROUTING TABLE is
the fan-out.
pub/sub cluster
133 nodes, consistent-
hash channel ring
WS server B
WS server N
5 delivered to every server subscribed to channel:{uid}
6 for each LOCAL client who is a friend of {uid}:
d = haversine(client.lastKnownPos, update.pos)
d <= client.radius ? send on that socket : drop
Filtering at the receiver costs 40 haversines spread over ~40 servers, each of which
already holds the relevant client's last position.
REST API servers STATELESS
friends, profile, settings,
history queries. Scale and
deploy normally.
user / friendship DB
sharded on user_id. Read on
CONNECT - the hot path never
touches it.
service discovery (ZooKeeper / etcd)
holds the channel -> node hash ring so every WS
server can compute which pub/sub node owns a
channel. Cached in-process, refreshed on change.
Deliberately NOT separated: there is no 'location service'
between the WS server and the cache. The WS server writes
the cache and publishes directly. An intermediate service
would add a hop to a path that runs 333,000 times a second
in order to do nothing but forward.
Why these are four services and not one
WS servers are STATEFUL
~100k live TCP connections each, plus per
connection a subscription set and a small
friends'-last-position cache. That state is
bound to the connection, so they cannot be
recycled like a stateless tier: scale-in
needs DRAINING and a deploy means 100,000
clients reconnecting.
REST servers are STATELESS
friends, profile, settings, history. Mixing
these into the WS tier would impose
connection-draining semantics on every
ordinary HTTP deploy.
pub/sub is sized by a DIFFERENT resource
2 nodes' worth of memory and 133 nodes'
worth of CPU. A component whose sizing is
driven purely by push throughput has
nothing operationally in common with one
holding connections.
the history sink is a different workload
1.15 TB/day durable append-only. Coupling a
write-heavy pipeline to the latency-sensitive
fan-out path would let the history store's
health affect the live feature.
The connect path - where the operational pain lives
1 authenticate
resolve user_id
2 GET /friends
from the user DB,
or a cached copy
3 SUBSCRIBE
to channel:{friend_id}
for EVERY friend
4 MGET loc:{friend}
one BULK read for
all friends
5 send init
distances for everyone
currently nearby
Step 3 is the expensive one: a client with 400 friends issues 400 subscriptions. So a deploy that reconnects 10M clients means
4 BILLION subscription operations - the design's worst operational moment, and the reason subscriptions are batched and
deploys are rolled slowly.
Step 4 exists precisely to close a race: a client that connects while a friend's update is in flight misses that publish,
because its server had not yet subscribed. The bulk read covers it - a newly connected client would otherwise see nothing
until each friend's next 30-second update.
One TTL doing three jobs - which is why there is no presence service
loc:{user_id} present -> the user is ACTIVE
loc:{user_id} expired -> inactive; disappears
bounds cache memory
bounds staleness
IS the presence mechanism
There is NO heartbeat, no presence service, and no 'user went offline' event to publish. 'Friends inactive for 10 minutes
disappear' is satisfied entirely by a TTL that had to exist anyway to bound memory. This is the design's cleanest
simplification - and it is only available because lossy, eventual semantics were accepted up front: a presence system with
delivery guarantees would need explicit online/offline events, ordering between them, and reconciliation when they are missed.
All 100M channels exist whether or not the user is online
pre-allocated at provisioning time
created on login, destroyed on logout
An idle Redis pub/sub channel with no subscribers
consumes no memory - it is a key in a routing table,
not a buffer. So the 205 GB figure is a worst-case
ceiling and the practical memory is far lower.
Trading a bounded, predictable memory ceiling for the
elimination of a coordination protocol is
straightforwardly correct.
Sounds tidier, and creates a real problem: every one of
that user's 400 friends' servers must be TOLD the channel
now exists so it can subscribe.
That is a distributed coordination event on every login,
40 subscription changes triggered by one connect, and a
race where a friend's update is published before a
subscriber has finished subscribing.
Backpressure hits the pub/sub nodes' CPU first - and the strongest lever costs nothing to build
suppress near-identical positions
if a user has not moved appreciably, publishing changes nothing on any screen.
The cheapest saving available, and it should be on permanently, not only under load.
raise the refresh interval from 30 s to 60 s
a server-controlled config change that HALVES THE ENTIRE WORKLOAD - writes and
pushes together - for a barely perceptible product change. By far the biggest lever.
drop pushes to clients with slow sockets
rather than buffering them: a buffered stale position is worse than no position.
NEVER shed the init bulk read on connect
a client with an empty screen looks broken; a client missing one update does not.
And the load profile is unusually benign: 333k/sec comes from a fixed 30-second timer over a slowly-varying population, so
there is no thundering-herd shape to absorb - the diurnal curve moves it maybe 3x. The real variable is the FAN-OUT
MULTIPLIER, and it is a SOCIAL parameter, not a technical one. If average friend counts rise, or an evening peak lifts the
online fraction from 10% to 25%, the push rate moves proportionally while the write rate does not budge. You can be perfectly
provisioned for writes and 2.5x under-provisioned for pushes, from a change in user behaviour with no change in traffic.
What breaks when each piece dies - note which one recovers fastest
a pub/sub node dies
its channels rehash; affected servers resubscribe
seconds of missed updates for ~1/133 of users
a WebSocket server dies
its ~100,000 clients reconnect elsewhere and re-subscribe
the SUBSCRIPTION STORM is the real cost, not the connection loss
the location cache dies
init returns empty, so users see nobody
THE FEATURE IS DOWN - and it recovers in one refresh interval (30 s)
the history pipeline dies
circuit breaker opens; the WS server drops history writes
zero user impact; an analytics gap
the friendship DB dies
existing connections keep working; NEW ones fail
they cannot resolve who to subscribe to - the hot path never touches it
The cache is the component whose loss is most visible AND the one that recovers fastest, because the data rebuilds itself.
Retries, meanwhile, are almost entirely absent by design: a failed push is not retried because the next update supersedes it,
and a failed cache write is not retried either. Retry queues at 13.3M pushes/sec would be a larger system than the one they
were protecting - so the fire-and-forget requirement shows up as an ABSENCE of machinery, and the absence is the point.
The sharpest edges, stated as edges
receiver-side filtering wastes most of the work a push is delivered to a friend's server and THEN discarded if they are
beyond the radius. For users with scattered friends, the overwhelming
majority of 13.3M pushes/sec are dropped after delivery. Geohash-prefixed
channels - publish to channel:{uid}:{geohash5}, subscribe only to nearby
prefixes - would filter BEFORE the push. The clear next optimization.
privacy is enforced only at the subscription boundary a server subscribes to a friend's channel and then filters by
distance, so it RECEIVES that friend's exact position even when they are
500 miles away and should be invisible. Nothing is shown to the user, but
the data crossed a boundary it did not need to. Geohash channels would fix
this as a side effect - a good argument for doing them on privacy grounds.
the whale problem is capped, not solved 5,000 friends means 500 pushes per update instead of 40, so that channel is
12x hotter. Consistent hashing spreads whale channels across nodes; a
friend-count limit is a product constraint standing in for an engineering
one, which is an uncomfortable place to leave it.
a full-fleet reconnect is a multi-minute recovery 4 billion subscriptions. Staggered reconnect with jitter, sticky routing
and batched subscribes reduce it and do not eliminate it.
